cards.title: EAFP: Easier to Ask Forgiveness Than Permission
cards.teaser: EAFP means trying an operation and handling the exception if it fails, rather than checking upfront whether the operation will succeed. Python's culture and runtime favor EAFP over LBYL (Look Before You Leap).

runs.text: LBYL (Look Before You Leap) checks preconditions before acting —
if key in d: return d[key]
. It is readable but has a race-condition flaw in concurrent code: the check and the act are two separate operations, and the world can change between them. EAFP collapses them into one:
is atomic — the dictionary either has the key or raises
, with no window for a race. Python's built-in types and idioms are designed around EAFP:
are all EAFP helpers under the hood.

items.text: when failures are genuinely exceptional — infrequent and hard to predict upfront.
when you want to produce a clear, early error message before an expensive or irreversible operation begins.

runs.text: EAFP maps to Python's optimistic execution model: CPython has no upfront type checking, so the interpreter is already structured around catching errors after the fact. EAFP aligns with how the runtime itself works.

EAFP is like trying a door instead of first checking whether it's unlocked. You just try it — if it opens, great; if it's locked, you handle that. One step instead of two, and you can't get a different result between the check and the try.

cards.title: Custom Exception Hierarchies
cards.teaser: Define your own exception classes, organized into a hierarchy rooted at a module-level base exception. Callers can catch the broad base or drill into specific subclasses — without coupling to your implementation details.

runs.text: works for simple cases, but gives callers no way to distinguish your library's errors from Python's own. A custom hierarchy fixes this: define a
at the top, then subclass it for specific conditions.

Use 'raise NewError(...) from original_error' to chain exceptions. Python preserves the original traceback under __cause__, and the error message shows 'The above exception was the direct cause of...', which is invaluable for debugging.

A custom exception hierarchy is a menu for your callers. The root exception is the "anything from this library went wrong" option. Subclasses are more specific dishes. Callers order what they need — broad or specific — without knowing your kitchen.

cards.title: Context Managers and the with Statement
cards.teaser: The with statement guarantees that a resource is cleaned up when a block exits — whether normally, by exception, or by return. It replaces the try/finally boilerplate that wraps every raw resource acquisition.

runs.text: block starts and returns the value bound to the
always runs when the block exits — it receives the exception type, value, and traceback if one occurred, and can suppress it by returning
statement works for any of them identically.

items.text: with open(a) as f, open(b) as g:
stacks two managers; both are cleaned up, in reverse order.

runs.text: Don't suppress exceptions in __exit__ unless you've genuinely handled them. Silently swallowing errors is one of the hardest bugs to diagnose — the failure happens in one place, but the symptom appears somewhere completely different.

with is a pair of guaranteed hooks around a block of code. Whatever happens inside — success, exception, or early return — the cleanup hook always fires. Think of it as a try/finally that Python writes for you.

cards.title: contextlib: Context Managers Without a Class
cards.teaser: The contextlib module turns a generator function into a context manager with @contextmanager — no class, no __enter__, no __exit__. Everything before yield is setup; everything after is teardown.

runs.text: Writing a full context manager class for every resource is verbose.
lets you write a generator instead: put setup before
target receives, then put teardown after. Wrap the yield in
if teardown must run even when the block raises.

items.text: — a context manager that silently swallows the listed exception types.
— dynamically manages a variable number of context managers; useful when the list of resources is determined at runtime.
— a no-op context manager for optional wrapping (Python 3.7+).

runs.text: ExitStack is the right tool when you're opening a list of files — 'with ExitStack() as stack: files = [stack.enter_context(open(p)) for p in paths]'. All files are guaranteed to close even if one open() or read() fails.

@contextmanager lets you write a context manager as a function with a yield in the middle. The code before the yield is the setup; the code after is the teardown. No class needed — just a function that pauses and resumes.

cards.title: Profiling with cProfile
cards.teaser: cProfile is Python's built-in deterministic profiler. It counts every function call and measures cumulative and per-call time, so you can find which function is actually responsible for slowness — not which one you suspected.

runs.text: replaces guessing with measurement. Run it with

items.text: — how many times the function was called; unexpectedly high counts reveal algorithmic inefficiency.
— cumulative time; useful for finding the top-level culprit.
— time in the function only; useful for finding the hot leaf.

runs.text: cProfile adds overhead (it instruments every call), so measured times are slower than production. Use it to find which function to optimize, then use timeit to measure the optimized version precisely.

cProfile is like a time-sheet for your program. Every function clocks in when called and clocks out when it returns. At the end you get a report showing exactly who spent the most time on the clock — no more guessing.

runs.text: Time profiling finds slow code; memory profiling finds code that grows the heap unnecessarily.

objects instead of reading line by line.
— returns the size of a single object in bytes (does not recurse into container contents).

runs.text: tracemalloc.get_traced_memory() returns (current, peak) bytes since start(). Use peak to find the high-water mark — the maximum RAM your code ever needed simultaneously.

tracemalloc is a receipt printer for memory. Every time your code allocates, it prints a line in the receipt. At the end you can sort the receipt by cost and see exactly which line of code spent the most bytes.

cards.title: __slots__ for Memory-Efficient Instances
cards.teaser: __slots__ replaces the per-instance __dict__ with a fixed set of descriptors, cutting instance memory by 40–60% and speeding up attribute access — at the cost of no dynamic attributes and no default pickling.

runs.text: By default, every Python instance stores its attributes in a
— a hash table that supports arbitrary keys. This is flexible but costly: a
adds roughly 200–400 bytes per instance. For classes that hold millions of objects (points in a point cloud, rows in a parsed CSV), that overhead dominates.
at the class level tells Python to allocate fixed slots instead of a dict. Attribute access becomes a C-level struct lookup — faster and smaller.

items.text: — cannot add undeclared attributes at runtime; subclasses that don't declare
— data classes with a fixed schema that are instantiated in bulk (millions of objects).

runs.text: Measure before adding __slots__. The savings are real but the restrictions are real too. If your class holds only a handful of instances, the complexity is not worth it.

__slots__ is like switching from a flexible backpack (a dictionary that can hold anything) to a fixed-pocket vest. Each pocket is labeled and sized exactly. You lose flexibility but gain speed and lose weight — ideal when you're carrying millions of them.

cards.title: weakref: References That Don't Prevent Garbage Collection
cards.teaser: A weak reference points to an object without incrementing its reference count. When nothing else holds the object alive, it is garbage-collected and the weak reference returns None — breaking reference cycles automatically.

runs.text: CPython's garbage collector is primarily reference-counting. An object is freed when its reference count reaches zero. But cycles — object A holds B, B holds A — keep both counts above zero forever, leaking memory.
breaks cycles by creating a reference that does not count.
if the object has been collected. Always check:

items.text: — a cache whose values are held weakly; entries disappear automatically when the value has no other references.
— a set whose members are held weakly; useful for observer/listener registries.

runs.text: Not all objects support weak references. Built-in types like int, str, tuple, and list do not. Classes must have __weakref__ in their slots (added automatically unless __slots__ omits it) to be weakly referenceable.

A weak reference is like a sticky note with an address — it tells you where the object lives, but it doesn't hold the building up. If everyone with a real key leaves, the building comes down regardless of how many sticky notes remain.

runs.text: Jupyter users: %timeit and %%timeit magic commands call timeit with auto-calibrated repeat/number counts and print a human-friendly summary. They are the fastest way to micro-benchmark interactively.

timeit is like timing a sprint by running it a thousand times and taking the fastest result. One run can be slow because of a red light (OS scheduler); a thousand runs lets the fastest, uninterrupted attempt speak for itself.

cards.title: Measure First: Avoiding Premature Optimization
cards.teaser: Premature optimization is optimizing code before measurements show it is actually a bottleneck. The cost is real: complex, hard-to-maintain code that is faster in the part that doesn't matter.

runs.text: Donald Knuth's full quote: "We should forget about small efficiencies, say about 97% of the time: premature optimization is the root of all evil. Yet we should not pass up our opportunities in that critical 3%." The implication: profiling is how you find the 3%. Without profiling you are guessing — and programmers guess wrong most of the time.

items.text: Make it fast where it matters.
Optimize only the bottleneck, then re-measure to verify improvement.

runs.text: Algorithm complexity matters more than micro-optimizations. Replacing an O(n²) scan with an O(n log n) sort or an O(1) hash lookup gives gains no amount of
or loop unrolling can match. Look at the big picture before micro-benchmarking.

When you do optimize, document why with a comment that includes the benchmark result. Future maintainers (including yourself) should know whether the trick is still necessary after Python or library versions change.

Premature optimization is polishing the door of a house that doesn't have a roof yet. Get the roof on — working code — then find the one door that actually needs polishing by measuring. The other 97% of doors can stay unpolished.

cards.title: CPython Performance Characteristics
cards.teaser: CPython's execution model — bytecode interpreted by a C loop, the GIL, dynamic dispatch for every attribute access — has predictable fast and slow patterns. Knowing them lets you write code that works with the interpreter, not against it.

runs.text: CPython compiles source to bytecode, then interprets that bytecode in a C

loop (the "eval loop"). Each bytecode instruction carries overhead: a type-dispatch, a stack push/pop, and often a dictionary lookup. This makes pure Python 10–100x slower than equivalent C — but the gap narrows when Python calls into C extensions.

items.text: run in C; prefer them over manual Python loops.
searches the MRO. Inside a hot loop, cache
Local variables are faster than globals
String concatenation in loops is O(n²)

runs.text: Python 3.11+ introduced the 'specializing adaptive interpreter' (PEP 659): the eval loop rewrites bytecode on the fly for frequently executed paths (e.g., always-int addition). Real-world benchmarks show 10–60% speedup over 3.10 with zero code changes.

CPython is a translator that reads your code word-by-word and runs the C equivalent for each word. The more words you eliminate — by using built-ins that speak C natively — the faster your program runs.

cards.title: The warnings Module for Deprecations
cards.teaser: The warnings module lets you alert callers that an API is deprecated or being used incorrectly — without raising an exception. Python filters duplicate warnings automatically so users are not spammed.

runs.text: When you rename a function or change a default argument, you have two choices: break callers immediately or give them a migration window with a deprecation warning.
points the warning at the caller's code, not at the line inside your library that called
. Without it, the warning shows the wrong file and line, making it hard for callers to find what to fix.

items.text: — shown only in __main__ and test runners by default. Use for APIs you plan to remove.
— shown to all users by default. Use for behavior changes that will affect everyone.
— for unusual but not necessarily wrong usage.
— turns warnings into exceptions; use in tests to catch deprecated API use.

runs.text: In pytest, add 'filterwarnings = error' to pytest.ini (or pyproject.toml [tool.pytest.ini_options]) to fail the test suite on any unhandled DeprecationWarning. This catches deprecated API usage before it reaches production.

warnings.warn() is a sticky note you leave on an API you're about to remove. It tells callers: 'This still works today, but update your code before the next release.' Python shows the note once per call site so it's visible without being noisy.
